```{r load-data, include=FALSE}
world_happiness <- read.csv("..//:data/world_happiness.csv")

# Handle missing values (replace with mean or remove rows if excessive)
world_happiness <- world_happiness %>% drop_na()

# Rename columns for clarity
world_happiness <- world_happiness %>% rename(
  Country = Country.name,
  Happiness_Rank = Rank,
  Happiness_Score = Ladder.score,
  Lower_Confidence = lowerwhisker,
  Upper_Confidence = upperwhisker,
  GDP_per_Capita = Explained.by..Log.GDP.per.capita,
  Social_Support = Explained.by..Social.support,
  Healthy_Life_Expectancy = Explained.by..Healthy.life.expectancy,
  Freedom_to_Choose = Explained.by..Freedom.to.make.life.choices,
  Corruption_Perception = Explained.by..Perceptions.of.corruption,
  Generosity = Explained.by..Generosity,
  Dystopia_Residual = Dystopia...residual
)

# Create new variable, Continent using the countrycode package
world_happiness <- world_happiness %>%
  mutate(
    Continent = countrycode(
      Country,
      origin = "country.name",
      destination = "continent",
      custom_match = c(
        "Kosovo" = "Europe", # Manual mappings
        "Taiwan Province of China" = "Asia",
        "Hong Kong SAR of China" = "Asia"
      )
    )
  )

# Custom diverging palette for continents
continent_colors <- c(
  "Europe" = "#d7191c", # Red
  "Oceania" = "#ffffbf", # Orange
  "Americas" = "#fdae61", # Yellow (light)
  "Africa" = "#abd9e9", # Light blue
  "Asia" = "#2c7bb6" # Dark blue
)

# Define custom colors for each year (2019 to 2024)
year_colors <- c(
  "2019" = "#8c510a", # Brownish Orange
  "2020" = "#d8b365", # Light Brown
  "2021" = "#f6e8c3", # Very Light Yellow
  "2022" = "#c7eae5", # Light Teal
  "2023" = "#5ab4ac", # Teal
  "2024" = "#01665e" # Dark Teal
)
```

## <div class="header-bar">Background</div>
.pull-left[
- **Happiness is a key indicator** of well-being, going beyond traditional economic measures.

- The World Happiness Report (2019–2024) dives into what really makes nations happy.

- A global survey, evaluates how income, social support, health, governance, and freedom affect happiness worldwide.

- The report ranks 150+ countries based on happiness scores, derived from multiple factors such as **Economic**, **Social**, **Health** and **Governance**.
]

```{r WER logo, echo=FALSE, out.width = "32%", fig.align="right"}
include_graphics("img/wer-logo.png")
```
--
---
## <div class="header-bar">Research Questions</div>
  
.pull-cen[
### Question 1

#### What are the most important economic, social, and governance factors influencing national happiness from 2019 to 2024, and how effectively can a statistical model capture their impact?
.pull-cen[
<strong>H₀</strong>: Economic, social, and governance predictors do not significantly affect happiness scores.

<strong>H₁</strong>: Economic, social, and governance predictors significantly affect happiness scores.
]

### Question 2
#### What distinguishes the happiest and least happy South Asian countries from 2019–2024, and where does Pakistan stand among them?

]
---
## <div class="header-bar">Data</div>
### Source
- An annual survey that measures the subjective well-being and happiness of people **across 150+ countries**

- Collected through the **Gallup World Poll**

- Data spans from **2019 to 2024**, covering annual trends.

### Data Cleaning and Preprocessing

* Missing values were removed using `na.omit()` to ensure data accuracy.

* Column names were standardized for clarity using `dplyr::rename()`.

* Continent variable was created with the `countrycode()` function to enable regional comparisons.

---

## <div class="header-bar">Question 1 - Approach</div>

.pull-cen[
#### Used multiple linear regression to measure how key factors influence happiness scores, quantifies each factor’s impact and tests our hypothesis.
]

.panelset.sideways[
.panel[.panel-name[Happiness Score - Distribution Plot] 
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=3, dpi=300}

  )
```

]

.panel[.panel-name[GDP per Capita - Distribution Plot] 
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo = FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4, dpi=300}
ggplot(world_happiness, aes(x = GDP_per_Capita)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "darkred", color = "black", alpha = 0.7) +

  ) +

```
.footnote[The histogram shows most countries have a mid-range GDP per capita, with fewer countries at the low or high extremes. The distribution is **slightly right-skewed**, indicating only a few nations enjoy much higher prosperity.]
]
.panel[.panel-name[Impact of Key Factors on Happiness] 
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo = FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4, dpi=300}
# Long format for faceting
world_cor_happiness <- world_happiness %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      GDP_per_Capita, Social_Support, Healthy_Life_Expectancy,
      Freedom_to_Choose, Generosity, Corruption_Perception
    ),
    names_to = "Factor", values_to = "Value"
  )

# Faceted plot to visualize correlation between Happiness Score and Contributing Factors
ggplot(world_cor_happiness, aes(x = Value, y = Happiness_Score, color = Continent)) +

  facet_wrap(~Factor, drop = TRUE) +
  # scale_color_manual(values = continent_colors) +
  scale_color_viridis(discrete = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Associations Between Happiness and Key Development Indicators",
    x = "Contributing Factors",
    y = "Happiness Score",
    color = "Continents"
  ) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 4))) +
  theme_gray() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 8, hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 8, hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.background = element_blank(),
    legend.key = element_blank()
  )
```
.footnote[**GDP, freedom, social support & life expectancy** are **strongest predictors of happiness**, especially in Europe and Oceania; generosity and corruption have weaker, more variable effects]
]
.panel[.panel-name[Model]
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo = FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=2, dpi=300}
model <- lm(
  Happiness_Score ~ GDP_per_Capita + Social_Support + Healthy_Life_Expectancy +
    Freedom_to_Choose + Corruption_Perception + Generosity,
  data = world_happiness
)

kable(summary(model)$coefficients, caption = "Regression Coefficients for Full Model", digits = 5)
```

.footnote[The **model was constructed with `lm()` function**, including GDP per capita, Social Support, Healthy Life Expectancy, Freedom to Choose, Corruption Perception, and Generosity as predictors of happiness scores.
]
]
]

## <div class="header-bar">Question 1 - Modelling & Results</div>

.panelset[

.panel[.panel-name[Multicollinearity]

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo = FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.5, dpi=300}
num_vars <- world_happiness %>%
  select(
    GDP_per_Capita, Social_Support,
    Healthy_Life_Expectancy, Freedom_to_Choose, Generosity,
    Corruption_Perception
  )
colnames(num_vars) <- c(
  "GDP",
  "Social\nSupport",
  "Life\nExpectancy",
  "Freedom\nto Choose",
  "Generosity",
  "Corruption\nPerception"
)
ggpairs(
  num_vars,
  # title = "Pairwise Plots for Happiness Score Predictors",
  upper = list(continuous = wrap("cor", size = 3, color = "#2E86C1")),
  lower = list(continuous = wrap("smooth", alpha = 0.4, color = "#4D4D4D")), # alpha added here
  diag = list(continuous = wrap("densityDiag", fill = "#F5B041"))
) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5, size = ),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 6, angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 6),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 5)
  )
```
.footnote[**Dropping variables** which are **highly correlated** with each other.]
]
.panel[.panel-name[Reduced Model]

- Dropped Life Expectancy and Social Support and **keeping GDP**, as it’s a more general and stable economic indicator.
- Keeping **Freedom to Choose, Generosity and Corruption Perception**, they have moderate and unique contributions.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo = FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.5, dpi=300}
reduced_model <- lm(Happiness_Score ~ GDP_per_Capita + Freedom_to_Choose + Corruption_Perception + Generosity, data = world_happiness)

kable(summary(reduced_model)$coefficients, caption = "Regression Coefficients for Reduced Model", digits = 5)
```
]

.panel[.panel-name[95% CI]
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo = FALSE, fig.width=12, fig.height=2, dpi=300}
# confint(reduced_model)

kable(confint(reduced_model), caption = "95% Confidence Intervals for Reduced Model Coefficients", digits = 3)
```

.footnote[- **All variables** retained in the **reduced model**, GDP per Capita, Freedom to Choose, Corruption Perception, and Generosity have **statistically significant effects on happiness scores**. 
- Their **95% confidence intervals do not include zero**, confirming their importance in predicting national happiness between 2019 and 2024.]

]

.panel[.panel-name[Diagnostic Plots]

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo = FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=1.25, dpi=300}
autoplot(reduced_model,
  smooth.colour = "red",
  smooth.size = 0.8,
  shape = 21,
  # colour = "grey30",
  size = 0.25,
  label.size = 1,
  label.hjust = 0.5,
  label.colour = "blue",
  ncol = 2
) +
  theme_gray(base_size = 4) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(size = 4, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 4),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 4),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(size = 0.15),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 4)
  )
```

.footnote[**Residuals are fairly evenly spread** with no strong curve, **supporting linearity**, though a slight downward trend suggests **minor non-linearity** may be present. Residuals largely follow the diagonal, suggesting **approximate normality**, with minor tail deviations. The red line is mostly flat, with consistent spread, suggesting constant variance holds reasonably well. **Points 435, 669, and 863** have **slightly higher leverage**, but **none exceed Cook’s distance** cutoff. No highly influential points detected. 
]

]
.panel[.panel-name[Outliers]

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo = FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=1.25, dpi=300}
# Calculate Cook’s Distance
cooksD <- cooks.distance(reduced_model)

# Set threshold: 4 / n
n <- nrow(world_happiness)
threshold <- 4 / n

# Bind Cook's D back to the data
cooks_df <- world_happiness %>%
  mutate(
    Cooks_Distance = cooksD,
    Row = row_number()
  ) %>%
  filter(Row %in% c(435, 669, 863)) %>%
  select(Row, Country, Year, Happiness_Score, Cooks_Distance)

# Display as table
kable(cooks_df, digits = 5, caption = "Outliers and Their Cook’s Distance Values")
```
The following countries were flagged as outliers based on residual and leverage diagnostics.
As shown in the table, **all Cook’s Distance values fall below the conventional threshold** (4/n), indicating they are not influential and were retained in the model.

<div class="middle-bar">Findings confirm the hypothesis: The reduced model shows that GDP, freedom, corruption perception, and generosity significantly predict happiness. Model diagnostics confirm validity, with no influential outliers detected. </div>
]
]

## <div class="header-bar">Question 2 - Approach</div>

.pull-cen[
#### Used ANOVA to compare top and bottom performers in South Asia to assess regional disparities and Pakistan’s position.
]

.panelset.sideways[
.panel[.panel-name[Happiness vs Predictors in SA]

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=2, dpi=300}
# Define South Asian countries
south_asia <- c(
  "Pakistan", "India", "Bangladesh", "Sri Lanka",
  "Nepal", "Bhutan", "Maldives", "Afghanistan"
)

south_asia_data <- world_happiness %>%
  filter(Country %in% south_asia)

# Group by Country and calculate mean happiness and mean of predictors
south_asia_avg <- south_asia_data %>%
  group_by(Country) %>%
  summarise(
    Avg_Happiness = mean(Happiness_Score, na.rm = TRUE),
    GDP_per_Capita = mean(GDP_per_Capita, na.rm = TRUE),
    Social_Support = mean(Social_Support, na.rm = TRUE),
    Healthy_Life_Expectancy = mean(Healthy_Life_Expectancy, na.rm = TRUE),
    Freedom = mean(Freedom_to_Choose, na.rm = TRUE),
    Generosity = mean(Generosity, na.rm = TRUE),
    Corruption = mean(Corruption_Perception, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# Categorize countries
south_asia_avg <- south_asia_avg %>%
  mutate(Category = case_when(
    Country %in% Country[order(-Avg_Happiness)][1:2] ~ "Top 2",
    Country %in% Country[order(Avg_Happiness)][1:2] ~ "Bottom 2",
    Country == "Pakistan" ~ "Pakistan",
    TRUE ~ "Others"
  ))

# Reshape data for faceted plotting
south_asia_cor_happiness <- south_asia_avg %>%
  select(
    Country, Avg_Happiness, GDP_per_Capita, Social_Support,
    Healthy_Life_Expectancy, Freedom, Generosity, Corruption
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(Country, Avg_Happiness),
    names_to = "Factor",
    values_to = "Value"
  )

# Create faceted scatter plot
ggplot(south_asia_cor_happiness, aes(x = Value, y = Avg_Happiness)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = Country), size = 1) +
  # geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "gray30") +
  facet_wrap(~Factor, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_color_viridis(discrete = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Associations Between Average Happiness and Predictors",
    x = "Predictors",
    y = "Happiness Score"
  ) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 1))) +
  theme_gray() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 8, face = "bold"),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 6, hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 5),
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 6, hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 4),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 6, face = "bold"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 6),
    legend.background = element_blank(),
    legend.key = element_blank(),
    legend.key.height = unit(0.7, "lines"),
    legend.key.width = unit(0.3, "lines")
  )
```
.footnote[**Generosity, social support, freedom, and healthy life expectancy** appear to have the **strongest positive associations**, whereas corruption and GDP show more moderate influence.]
]

.panel[.panel-name[Correlation Matrix]

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=6, dpi=300}
# Select only numeric predictor columns + happiness
cor_data <- south_asia_avg %>%
  select(
    Avg_Happiness, GDP_per_Capita, Social_Support, Healthy_Life_Expectancy,
    Freedom, Generosity, Corruption
  )

# Compute correlation matrix
cor_matrix <- cor(cor_data, use = "complete.obs")

# Show only correlations with happiness
cor_with_happiness <- cor_matrix["Avg_Happiness", -1]

# Convert to tidy format for display
cor_df <- data.frame(
  # Predictor = names(cor_with_happiness),
  Correlation = round(cor_with_happiness, 3)
) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(Correlation)))


knitr::kable(cor_df, caption = "Correlation Matrix of Predictors with Average Happiness (South Asia)", digits = 3)
```
.footnote[Generosity and Social Support are most strongly correlated with happiness among South Asian countries in the dataset. **GDP**, surprisingly, is **less strongly linked** compared to social or emotional factors.]
]

.panel[.panel-name[Modeling Happiness in South Asia]

Three linear regression models were tested: 
- Model 1 included Generosity
- Model 2 added Social Support
- Model 3 incorporated all predictors

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=6, dpi=300}
# Model 1: Happiness ~ Generosity
model1 <- lm(Avg_Happiness ~ Generosity, data = south_asia_avg)


# Model 2: Happiness ~ Generosity + Social Support
model2 <- lm(Avg_Happiness ~ Generosity + Social_Support, data = south_asia_avg)

# Model 3: Generosity + Social Support + Healthy Life Expectancy
model3 <- lm(Avg_Happiness ~ Generosity + Social_Support + Healthy_Life_Expectancy + Freedom + GDP_per_Capita + Corruption, data = south_asia_avg)

# Extract
model_summary <- tibble(
  Model = c("Model 1", "Model 2", "Model 3"),
  Predictors = c(
    "Generosity",
    "Generosity + Social Support",
    "All Predictors"
  ),
  R_sq = c(
    summary(model1)$r.squared,
    summary(model2)$r.squared,
    summary(model3)$r.squared
  ),
  Adj_R = c(
    summary(model1)$adj.r.squared,
    summary(model2)$adj.r.squared,
    summary(model3)$adj.r.squared
  ),
  DF = c(
    df.residual(model1),
    df.residual(model2),
    df.residual(model3)
  ),
  p_value = c(
    summary(model1)$fstatistic %>%
      {
        pf(.[1], .[2], .[3], lower.tail = FALSE)
      },
    anova(model1, model2)$"Pr(>F)"[2],
    anova(model2, model3)$"Pr(>F)"[2]
  )
)

# Display as a formatted table
knitr::kable(model_summary, digits = 4, caption = "Comparison of Regression Models")
```
.footnote[**Model 1 (Generosity)** is statistically significant (**p = 0.0177**) and explains **64% of the variance in happiness**. Before drawing final conclusions about the best model, ANOVA will be performed to statistically test whether the additional predictors in Models 2 and 3 significantly improve the model fit compared to Model 1.]
]

]

## <div class="header-bar">Question 2 - Modelling & Results</div>

.panelset[

.panel[.panel-name[ANOVA on models]
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=6, dpi=300}
anova_res <- anova(model1, model2)
colnames(anova_res) <- c("Residual DF", "RSS", "DF", "Sum Sq", "F-value", "p-value")
kable(anova_res, digits = 4, caption = "ANOVA: Model 1 vs Model 2")

anova_res <- anova(model2, model3)
colnames(anova_res) <- c("Residual DF", "RSS", "DF", "Sum Sq", "F-value", "p-value")
kable(anova_res, digits = 4, caption = "ANOVA: Model 2 vs Model 3")
```
.footnote[Based on both model performance metrics and ANOVA results, **Model 1 (Generosity only)** is the most **statistically valid model**, with strong significance (**p = 0.0177**). Adding more predictors did not significantly improve the model.]
]

.panel[.panel-name[Actual vs Predicted - Model 1]

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo = FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=2, dpi=300}
# Add predicted values to the dataset
south_asia_avg$Predicted_Happiness <- predict(model1)

# Add residuals (optional, to show error)
south_asia_avg$Residual <- south_asia_avg$Avg_Happiness - south_asia_avg$Predicted_Happiness


# Create a flag for Pakistan
south_asia_avg$Highlight <- ifelse(south_asia_avg$Country == "Pakistan", "Pakistan", "Other")

# Plot
ggplot(south_asia_avg, aes(x = Predicted_Happiness, y = Avg_Happiness, label = Country)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = Highlight), size = 3) +
  geom_text(vjust = -1, hjust = 0.5, size = 2, fontface = "bold") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Pakistan" = "#d95f02", "Other" = "steelblue")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(2, 6)) +
  labs(
    title = "Actual vs Predicted Happiness (Model 1: Generosity)",
    x = "Predicted Happiness",
    y = "Actual Happiness"
  ) +
  theme_gray() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 8, hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 8, hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "none"
  )
```
.footnote[**Pakistan performs better** than predicted based on Generosity alone, suggesting the influence of additional unmodeled factors. Countries like India and Afghanistan, lie below the prediction line, indicating underperformance.]
]

.panel[.panel-name[Quantify Residuals]

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo = FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=2, dpi=300}
# Residual = Actual - Predicted
south_asia_avg$Residual <- south_asia_avg$Avg_Happiness - south_asia_avg$Predicted_Happiness

# Bar plot: Residuals (Actual - Predicted)
south_asia_avg %>%
  mutate(Country = reorder(Country, Residual)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Country, y = Residual, fill = Country == "Pakistan")) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#d95f02", "FALSE" = "steelblue"), guide = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals: Actual - Predicted Happiness (Model 1)",
    y = "Residual (Actual - Predicted)",
    x = "Country"
  ) +
  theme_gray() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 8, hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 8, hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.background = element_blank(),
    legend.key = element_blank()
  )
```
<div class="middle-bar">The results confirm that generosity, life expectancy, and freedom are key predictors of happiness in South Asia. Pakistan, ranked in the upper-middle tier, exceeded its predicted score, suggesting influence from additional unmodeled factors.</div>
]

]
---
## <div class="header-bar">Conclusion</div>


.pull-cen[

**Happiness is a multidimensional outcome influenced by more than just economic factors. While GDP does play a role, my analysis shows that social support, emotional well-being, and good governance are equally important, particularly in regions like South Asia, where these non-economic factors often have a stronger impact on overall life satisfaction.**
